title: Restlessness, confusion, or seeing/hearing people not present

source_packet.source_basis: Public-source synthesis for schema testing; no private testimony, no contributor interview, no claim of corpus completeness.
limitations: This pilot deliberately separates delirium, dreams/visions, and cultural/spiritual interpretation rather than collapsing them.
No claim is made about the meaning or reality-status of any experience.
Family-facing and clinical sources frame these phenomena differently.

moment.plain_scene: A person near death may become restless, confused, less alert, or may speak of seeing or hearing people or things not visible to others, including sometimes deceased loved ones.
ordinary_language_queries: talking to people not there before dying

content_layers.observation_text: Public sources describe terminal delirium, restlessness, confusion, and experiences of seeing or hearing people or things not present. NCI distinguishes hallucinations not related to delirium as occurring at end of life, while Hospice UK notes that some people may appear confused or see/hear pets or deceased people.
content_layers.source_synthesis: The sources support a careful crosswalk: some episodes may be clinically framed as delirium or restlessness, while other end-of-life experiences are discussed separately and may require family, spiritual, or chaplaincy support. The record must not force a single interpretation.

interpretation.editor_interpretation: This is one of the corpus's most important interpretation-separation cases. Families may experience these moments as frightening, meaningful, comforting, confusing, or sacred. A record must preserve observed words and setting without declaring what the dying person 'really' saw.

what_this_is_not: not proof of a universal spiritual event
not proof that the person is 'just confused'
not a reason to argue with or correct the dying person by default
not a clinical diagnosis without context
uncertainties: The boundary between delirium, dreams/visions, culture, and family meaning is complex.
Public sources do not provide the needed lived vocabulary across traditions.
Clinical assessment may matter when agitation, distress, pain, urinary retention, constipation, medication effects, or safety concerns are present.
content_layers.lay_orientation: A lay surface should avoid deciding the meaning. It should say that such reports are described in end-of-life sources, can be upsetting or meaningful, and active distress or agitation should be discussed with the care team.
content_layers.practitioner_notes: A practitioner surface should collect when to involve clinical staff, chaplaincy, family language, and cultural humility; it should also gather what experienced workers say when families ask whether the person is hallucinating or seeing the dead.
language_notes: Ordinary-language search phrases are retained as search aliases, not as diagnostic labels.
Professional terms are index handles; they do not collapse all contexts into one cause or one meaning.

provenance.provenance_statement: Drafted from named public sources to test the v2 witnessed-moment schema. It should be reviewed before any public surface uses it.

safety.clinical_boundary: This record is observational/source-indexing only. It is not medical advice, not a prognosis, and not a substitute for a local hospice, clinician, emergency, or care team.
safety.safety_notes: Before public use, route through clinical safety review and ensure lay surface directs urgent or worried readers to qualified local support.
